patient.name: Chantelle Williams
patient.setting: GP surgery, then Tier 3 weight management clinic
patient.complaint: Breathless climbing stairs and exhausted during the day; wants help losing weight
background: Type 2 diabetes diagnosed 3 years ago, on metformin
Hopes to have a baby in the next few years; care worker in Croydon

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' where obesity is the clue to a complication (OSA, GORD/Barrett's, NAFLD, pre-diabetes), or a BMI to classify, or a child whose obesity has an underlying cause.

points: Breathless on stairs; struggles to walk far.
Partner says she **snores loudly and stops breathing** at night.
Heartburn most evenings, worse lying down.

steps.q: Chantelle weighs 118 kg and is 1.68 m tall. How is her weight classified?

steps.lead: Chantelle's BMI of **41.8** puts her in the **severe obesity** band.
For Chantelle it is diet, inactivity and family genetics. In a **child**, always look for an underlying cause.
Chantelle's **breathlessness and reduced mobility** are typical; many people have no symptoms at all.
Chantelle already has **T2DM** and **hypertension**; her snoring suggests **OSA** and her heartburn **GORD**.

Childhood obesity: is there an underlying cause?

steps.text: A **short** obese child has an endocrine or genetic cause until proven otherwise; simple obesity usually makes children **taller**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' for BMI (percentile in children), waist circumference for cardiovascular risk, baseline HbA1c and lipids, and a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks in pregnancy with BMI ≥30.

steps.lead: Chantelle's diagnosis is her **BMI** plus clinical assessment; a child would need a **BMI percentile** for age and sex.

points: Epworth score 15; sleep study confirms **moderate OSA**.
She asks what happens to screening if she becomes pregnant.

steps.lead: Chantelle is screened for **CVD, T2DM, OSA and NAFLD**. In pregnancy, BMI ≥30 means a **75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks**.

steps.q: If Chantelle becomes pregnant with BMI ≥30, which test screens for gestational diabetes?
steps.r: BMI ≥30 is a risk factor, so she has a **75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks**.

steps.text: Adult BMI cut-offs do **not** apply to children. Use the **BMI percentile** for age and sex.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' as a BMI ladder: lifestyle for all, orlistat or GLP-1 mimetic by BMI and comorbidity, Tier 3 referral, then bariatric surgery (first-line if BMI >50). Know the GLP-1 stopping rule.

steps.lead: Chantelle starts with **lifestyle**: calorie deficit, more activity and behavioural support. Children get **family-based** programmes.

steps.title: The BMI ladder
nodes: Lifestyle and behavioural programme for all

steps.lead: BMI 41.8 with T2DM: Chantelle is referred to the **Tier 3 Specialist Weight Management Service**.

steps.q: Tier 3 starts semaglutide. What side effect must Chantelle report immediately?
steps.r: Severe upper abdominal pain suggests **pancreatitis**, the key GLP-1 mimetic side effect.

steps.lead: With BMI >35 and T2DM, Chantelle qualifies for a **GLP-1 mimetic**; it stops if she loses **<5%** after 12 weeks at maximum dose.

visual.title: Chantelle's weight on semaglutide
visual.caption: She lost 3.8 kg (**3.2%**): under the **5%** threshold, so semaglutide is stopped.

points: Her T2DM is **3 years old** (under 10 years).
She is listed for a **gastric bypass**.

steps.text: Bariatric surgery: BMI >35 with **recent-onset T2DM** (<10 years) or BMI >40 without comorbidity; **first-line if BMI >50**.

steps.lead: Long-term Chantelle needs **relapse prevention**, and before any pregnancy, **folic acid**; if BMI stays >35, **aspirin** from 12 weeks.
Chantelle's pathway follows **NICE CG189** and NICE bariatric surgery guidance.

steps.text: Do not jump to drugs or surgery without **lifestyle first**: every SBA ladder starts with diet, activity and behavioural support.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: how orlistat and GLP-1 mimetics work, why visceral fat causes insulin resistance, why obesity causes OSA and GORD, and why bariatric surgery improves diabetes before much weight is lost.

steps.lead: Chantelle's weight gain is years of **positive energy balance**: more energy in than out, so fat stores expand.
Chantelle's **visceral** fat releases less **adiponectin** and more **TNF-alpha and IL-6**, making her **insulin resistant**.

steps.title: Visceral fat to type 2 diabetes
nodes: Insulin resistance in muscle and liver

steps.lead: Fat around Chantelle's **upper airway** narrows it in sleep (OSA); raised **intra-abdominal pressure** pushes acid up (GORD).
Semaglutide mimics the **incretin GLP-1**; orlistat blocks **lipases** so dietary fat passes unabsorbed.

Mechanism
Classic side effect

mcq.q: Obesity increases the risk of Barrett's oesophagus via which condition?
mcq.r: Obesity causes **GORD**, which can lead to Barrett's oesophagus.

mcq.q: Which syndrome causes childhood obesity with hyperphagia and neonatal hypotonia?
mcq.r: **Prader-Willi**; Down, hypothyroidism and Cushing's are other listed causes.

mcq.q: Above which waist circumference is CV risk increased in men?
mcq.r: **94 cm in men, 80 cm in women**.

mcq.q: How is obesity diagnosed in a child?
o: BMI percentile for age and sex
mcq.r: **BMI percentile** adjusted for age and gender.

mcq.q: Which test screens for gestational diabetes in a woman with BMI ≥30?
When should a GLP-1 mimetic be stopped?
o: <5% weight loss after 12 weeks at maximum dose
mcq.r: Stop if **<5%** of initial weight is lost after **12 weeks at maximum dose** (or 6 months).

mcq.q: At what BMI is bariatric surgery a first-line option?
Which serious side effect of GLP-1 mimetics presents with upper abdominal pain?

mcq.r: **Lipase inhibition** reduces fat digestion and absorption.

technique.stem: A 48 year old man has a 6 month history of burning retrosternal pain after meals that is worse when lying flat. He has an acid taste in his mouth at night. He has no weight loss, dysphagia or vomiting. His BMI is 37 kg/m². His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of retrosternal pain in an obese man: think about what obesity predisposes to.

clues: acid taste in his mouth at night
no weight loss, dysphagia or vomiting
steps.x: Classic reflux symptoms; no red flags; **obesity** raises intra-abdominal pressure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **GORD**, driven by obesity.

elim: Achalasia gives dysphagia to solids and liquids, and regurgitation.
Cancer gives progressive dysphagia and weight loss.
Peptic ulcer pain is epigastric and linked to food timing, not lying flat.
Angina is exertional, not postprandial and positional.

steps.x: **B. GORD.** Rule: obesity is a risk factor for GORD and, through it, Barrett's.

technique.stem: A 9 year old girl is brought to the GP by her mother, who is worried about her weight. She is tall for her age and developing normally. She eats large portions and plays video games most evenings. Her weight is 52 kg and her height is 1.42 m.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm that she is obese?
o: BMI percentile adjusted for age and sex

steps.x: How to **diagnose** obesity in a child.
A child, so adult cut-offs do not apply; tall stature suggests **simple** obesity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **BMI percentile** for age and sex.

elim: Adult BMI bands are not valid in children.
Skinfold thickness is not the standard test.
Adult waist cut-offs (80/94 cm) do not apply.
Weight alone ignores height.

steps.x: **B. BMI percentile adjusted for age and sex.** Rule: adults = BMI; children = BMI percentile.

technique.stem: A 50 year old woman has a BMI of 29 kg/m² and hypertension. She has followed a structured diet and activity programme for 6 months without losing weight. She does not have diabetes. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg on ramipril.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Next step after lifestyle failure: where is she on the BMI ladder?
BMI >28 **with a comorbidity**, after lifestyle has failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Orlistat**.

elim: Surgery needs BMI >35 with comorbidity or >40.
GLP-1 mimetics are for BMI >35, or >30 with comorbidities.
Tier 3 is for BMI >35 with comorbidities or >40.
She has already tried lifestyle properly.

steps.x: **C. Orlistat.** Rule: BMI >28 + comorbidity + lifestyle failed = orlistat.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 44 kg/m² has a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. One week after surgery her fasting glucose has fallen markedly and her insulin dose is reduced, although she has lost only 3 kg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the early improvement in her glycaemic control?

steps.x: A mechanism: why glucose improves before much weight loss.
The effect is too early to be weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Altered gut hormones: **raised GLP-1 and PYY**.

elim: Glucagon would raise glucose.
Leptin changes follow fat loss.
Bypass does not cause major carbohydrate malabsorption.
Not the recognised mechanism.

steps.x: **A. Increased GLP-1 and PYY.** Rule: bariatric surgery improves glucose independent of weight loss via gut hormones.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man is brought by his wife, who says he snores loudly and stops breathing for several seconds at night. He falls asleep while watching television and nearly fell asleep driving. His BMI is 39 kg/m² and his collar size is 19 inches. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 152/94 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness in an obese man with a large neck is obstructive sleep apnoea, caused by fat deposition in the upper airway.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a sleepy obese man.
Witnessed apnoeas, daytime somnolence, obesity, large neck.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Obstructive sleep apnoea**, an obesity complication.

elim: Central apnoea is from heart failure or opioids, without snoring.
Hypothyroidism has other features such as cold intolerance.
Narcolepsy has cataplexy and no apnoeas.
Obesity hypoventilation needs daytime hypercapnia, not given.

steps.x: **E. Obstructive sleep apnoea.** Rule: obesity + snoring + witnessed apnoeas + sleepiness = OSA.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman attends a health check. She weighs 112 kg and is 1.65 m tall. She has no symptoms and no medical history. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate classification of her weight?
practice.e: BMI = 112 ÷ 1.65² = 41.1 kg/m², which is severe obesity (≥40). Obesity is ≥30 and overweight 25 to 29.9.

steps.x: A classification: calculate the BMI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ≥40 = **severe obesity**.

elim: Healthy is 18.5 to 24.9.
Obesity is 30 to 39.9; she is above 40.
Overweight is 25 to 29.9.
Underweight is below 18.5.

steps.x: **D. Severe obesity.** Rule: 25 overweight, 30 obesity, 40 severe obesity.

practice.stem: A 46 year old man with a BMI of 36 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes has abnormal liver function tests at his diabetes review. He drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. He has no symptoms. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 140/88 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a diffusely bright, echogenic liver.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Obesity and type 2 diabetes with raised ALT, minimal alcohol, negative viral serology, normal ferritin and a bright liver on ultrasound is NAFLD, a complication of obesity.

steps.x: Diagnosis of abnormal LFTs in an obese diabetic.
Metabolic risk, little alcohol, fatty liver on ultrasound; ALT > AST.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **NAFLD**.

elim: 4 units a week is far too little.
Autoimmune hepatitis affects young women with very high ALT and autoantibodies.
Ferritin is normal.
PBC is cholestatic (high ALP) in middle-aged women.

steps.x: **D. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.** Rule: obesity + T2DM + raised ALT + no alcohol = NAFLD.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with a BMI of 38 kg/m² has had heartburn most days for 15 years. He has taken over-the-counter antacids but never seen a doctor. He has no dysphagia or weight loss. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. Upper GI endoscopy shows salmon-pink mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Long-standing reflux in an obese man with salmon-pink columnar mucosa above the GOJ is Barrett's oesophagus. Obesity causes GORD and, through it, Barrett's.

steps.x: Diagnosis from the endoscopy appearance.
Obesity → chronic GORD → columnar metaplasia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Barrett's oesophagus**.

elim: Candida gives white plaques, usually when immunosuppressed.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis gives rings and food bolus obstruction in young atopic men.
A hiatus hernia is a herniated stomach, not pink mucosa above the GOJ.
Cancer gives a mass with dysphagia and weight loss.

steps.x: **A. Barrett's oesophagus.** Rule: obesity → GORD → Barrett's (salmon-pink mucosa).

practice.stem: An 8 year old boy is referred with obesity. He was floppy and fed poorly as a baby, but now has an insatiable appetite and takes food from bins. He has learning difficulties, small hands and feet, and is short for his age. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his obesity?
practice.e: Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding followed by hyperphagia, learning difficulty, short stature and small hands and feet is Prader-Willi syndrome. Normal TSH and cortisol suppression exclude hypothyroidism and Cushing's.

steps.x: The cause of childhood obesity: is it simple or secondary?

clues: floppy and fed poorly as a baby
learning difficulties, small hands and feet
steps.x: Short stature means secondary; hypotonia then **hyperphagia** is classic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prader-Willi syndrome**.

elim: Cortisol suppresses normally.
Down syndrome has characteristic facies, not this hyperphagia pattern.
TSH is normal.
Simple obesity makes children tall, without these features.

steps.x: **D. Prader-Willi syndrome.** Rule: short obese child = look for a cause; hypotonia + hyperphagia = Prader-Willi.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman with a BMI of 34 kg/m² and a waist circumference of 104 cm has routine bloods. She has no thirst or polyuria. She has velvety dark skin in her axillae. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol (and fasting glucose 6.1 to 6.9) is pre-diabetes, a direct complication of obesity-driven insulin resistance; acanthosis nigricans supports insulin resistance. T2DM needs HbA1c ≥48.

steps.x: Diagnosis from glucose tests: place the numbers against the cut-offs.

clues: velvety dark skin in her axillae
steps.x: Central obesity and **acanthosis nigricans** = insulin resistance; HbA1c 45.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HbA1c 42 to 47 = **pre-diabetes**.

elim: LADA is autoimmune and progresses to insulin need; not suggested.
HbA1c and fasting glucose are both raised.
Type 1 presents with weight loss and ketones.
T2DM needs HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol.

steps.x: **C. Pre-diabetes.** Rule: obesity → insulin resistance → pre-diabetes (HbA1c 42–47) → T2DM.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman attends her booking appointment at 10 weeks of gestation in her first pregnancy. Her BMI is 34 kg/m². She has no history of diabetes. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to screen for gestational diabetes?
o: 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24–28 weeks
Urine dipstick for glucose at each visit
practice.e: BMI ≥30 is a risk factor for gestational diabetes, so she is offered a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks. Urine glucose and HbA1c are not reliable screening tests in pregnancy.

steps.x: A screening test for gestational diabetes in an obese pregnant woman.
BMI ≥30 = risk factor; no prior GDM.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks**.

elim: A single fasting glucose at booking misses later GDM.
HbA1c is unreliable in pregnancy and 36 weeks is too late.
Random glucose is not the screening test.
Glycosuria is common and unreliable in pregnancy.

steps.x: **A. 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks.** Rule: BMI ≥30 in pregnancy = OGTT at 24–28 weeks.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man has a BMI of 29 kg/m². He is a non-smoker with no medical history. His GP wants to assess whether his fat distribution places him at increased cardiovascular risk. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate measurement?
practice.e: Waist circumference measures central (visceral) fat; above 94 cm in men (80 cm in women) indicates increased cardiovascular risk. The other tests are not used in routine practice.

steps.x: A measurement of **fat distribution** for CV risk.
BMI alone does not show where the fat is.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Waist circumference** (>94 cm men).

elim: Impedance estimates total fat, not distribution.
DEXA is a research or specialist tool.
Neck size relates to OSA risk.
Skinfolds measure subcutaneous, not visceral, fat.

steps.x: **E. Waist circumference.** Rule: >94 cm men, >80 cm women = increased CV risk.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has a BMI of 31 kg/m². He has no hypertension, diabetes or other weight-related conditions. He has never tried a structured weight loss programme. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Lifestyle is first-line for all; adults without weight-related conditions are referred to a behavioural weight management programme. Drugs and surgery come later.

steps.x: Initial management: start at the bottom of the ladder.

clues: no hypertension, diabetes or other weight-related conditions
never tried a structured weight loss programme
steps.x: Obese, no comorbidity, no previous lifestyle attempt.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Behavioural weight management programme**.

elim: Surgery needs BMI >40, or >35 with comorbidity.
Orlistat follows lifestyle failure.
GLP-1 mimetics need BMI >35 or >30 with comorbidities.
Tier 3 is for BMI >35 with comorbidity or >40.

steps.x: **B. Behavioural weight management programme.** Rule: lifestyle first, always.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes started semaglutide in a specialist weight management service. She has now been on the maximum dose for 12 weeks. She tolerates it well. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase semaglutide above the licensed dose
practice.e: She has lost 3 kg (2.9%), less than 5% of initial body weight after 12 weeks at maximum dose, so the GLP-1 mimetic is stopped.

steps.x: A review decision on a GLP-1 mimetic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: <5% after 12 weeks at max dose = **stop**.

elim: Adding orlistat is not the rule-based next step.
The stopping rule has been met.
Never exceed the licensed dose.
Switching within the class is not recommended for non-response.

steps.x: **D. Stop semaglutide.** Rule: <5% weight loss after 12 weeks at maximum dose = stop.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man has a BMI of 53 kg/m². He has hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea. He is motivated and fit for anaesthesia. He has no psychiatric or eating disorder. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 148/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Very low calorie diet for 12 months
practice.e: With a BMI above 50, bariatric surgery can be offered as a first-line option, via the specialist service. Drugs and lifestyle alone are unlikely to be enough.

steps.x: Management for a very high BMI.
BMI >50 with comorbidities, fit for surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bariatric surgery** first-line.

elim: Lifestyle continues but alone is inadequate at BMI >50.
Drugs can bridge but surgery is first-line here.
Orlistat gives modest loss only.
Prolonged very low calorie diets are not recommended.

steps.x: **A. Bariatric surgery.** Rule: BMI >50 = surgery can be first-line.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman with a BMI of 33 kg/m² and hypertension starts a new weight-loss drug. Two weeks later she reports oily, loose, foul-smelling stools and faecal urgency, especially after fatty meals. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of her new drug?
o: Inhibition of pancreatic and gastric lipase
Inhibition of SGLT2 in the proximal tubule
practice.e: Oily stools after fatty meals mean dietary fat is not being absorbed: orlistat inhibits pancreatic and gastric lipases, reducing triglyceride hydrolysis and fat absorption.

steps.x: A drug mechanism explained by the side effect.
**Steatorrhoea**: undigested fat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Orlistat: **lipase inhibition**.

elim: GLP-1 mimetics cause nausea, not steatorrhoea.
Not a current weight-loss drug mechanism in the notes.
SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria and thrush.
PYY rises after bariatric surgery; no drug does this here.

steps.x: **C. Inhibition of pancreatic and gastric lipase.** Rule: oily stools = orlistat = lipase inhibitor.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: lifestyle is always the first rung.

points.p: Lifestyle for all: calorie deficit, activity, behavioural support
Children: family-involved lifestyle interventions

prompts.q: When are orlistat, GLP-1 mimetics and bariatric surgery used, and when is a GLP-1 stopped?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the BMI and comorbidities to the rung.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: obesity changes antenatal prescribing.

Folic acid from before conception to end of 1st trimester

Visceral fat: low adiponectin, leptin resistance, raised TNF-alpha/IL-6
Upper airway fat → OSA
Raised intra-abdominal pressure → GORD

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link each drug to its side effect.

points.p: GLP-1: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon
points.why: Incretin mimetic, low hypoglycaemia risk alone.

Orlistat: inhibits pancreatic/gastric lipase
Bariatric surgery raises GLP-1 and PYY

glossary.BMI: Body mass index: weight in kg divided by height in metres squared.
glossary.BMI percentile: Where a child's BMI sits compared with children of the same age and sex.
glossary.Waist circumference: Measure of central fat; above 94 cm in men or 80 cm in women means raised CV risk.
glossary.Visceral adiposity: Fat stored around the abdominal organs, the most metabolically harmful type.
glossary.Positive energy balance: Energy intake persistently exceeding energy expenditure, so fat stores grow.
glossary.Adipokines: Hormones and signals released by fat tissue, such as adiponectin and leptin.
glossary.Adiponectin: Fat-derived hormone that improves insulin sensitivity; low in obesity.
glossary.Leptin: Fat-derived satiety hormone; obese people become resistant to its effect.
glossary.TNF-alpha: Inflammatory cytokine released by visceral fat that worsens insulin resistance.
glossary.IL-6: Interleukin-6; inflammatory cytokine from fat tissue that contributes to insulin resistance.
glossary.Insulin resistance: Reduced response of tissues to insulin, so more insulin is needed to control glucose.
glossary.Acanthosis nigricans: Velvety dark skin in skin folds; a sign of insulin resistance.
glossary.Pre-diabetes: Glucose above normal but below the diabetes cut-off (HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol).
glossary.GORD: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: stomach acid refluxing into the oesophagus.
glossary.Barrett's oesophagus: Columnar metaplasia of the lower oesophagus from chronic reflux; pre-malignant.
glossary.OSA: Obstructive sleep apnoea: repeated upper airway collapse during sleep.
glossary.Epworth score: Questionnaire scoring daytime sleepiness; used when OSA is suspected.
glossary.NAFLD: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: fat build-up in the liver without heavy drinking.
glossary.Dyslipidaemia: Abnormal blood lipids, such as high triglycerides and low HDL.
glossary.Prader-Willi syndrome: Genetic syndrome with neonatal hypotonia, then hyperphagia, obesity and learning difficulty.
glossary.Cushing's syndrome: Excess cortisol causing central obesity, striae and hypertension.
glossary.OGTT: Oral glucose tolerance test: glucose measured 2 hours after a 75 g glucose drink.
glossary.Behavioural weight management programme: Structured group or individual programme supporting diet, activity and habit change.
glossary.Orlistat: Lipase inhibitor that reduces fat absorption; causes oily stools.
glossary.Lipase: Enzyme that breaks down dietary triglycerides so fat can be absorbed.
glossary.Steatorrhoea: Pale, oily, foul-smelling stools from unabsorbed fat.
glossary.GLP-1: Glucagon-like peptide-1, a gut incretin hormone that boosts insulin and reduces appetite.
glossary.GLP-1 mimetic: Injected GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g. semaglutide) used for weight loss and diabetes.
glossary.Semaglutide: Weekly GLP-1 mimetic for weight loss; stop if under 5% loss at 12 weeks on maximum dose.
glossary.Liraglutide: Daily GLP-1 mimetic used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes.
glossary.Tirzepatide: Dual GIP and GLP-1 agonist injection used for weight loss.
glossary.Incretin: Gut hormone released after eating that boosts glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
glossary.PYY: Peptide YY: gut hormone that reduces appetite; rises after bariatric surgery.
glossary.Pancreatitis: Inflammation of the pancreas with severe upper abdominal pain; a GLP-1 mimetic side effect.
glossary.Bariatric surgery: Weight-loss surgery such as gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy.
glossary.Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: Bariatric operation creating a small stomach pouch joined directly to the small bowel.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, an injected anticoagulant used to prevent VTE.
glossary.Factor V Leiden: Inherited mutation making blood more likely to clot.
glossary.Folic acid: B vitamin taken before and in early pregnancy to reduce neural tube defects.
